nameStory: The pumpkinseed gets its name from its distinctive orange-red ear flap that resembles the bright color of a pumpkin seed. When you see one swimming in shallow water, that vibrant orange 'ear' catches your eye just like finding a glossy pumpkin seed in your Halloween jack-o'-lantern. Some folks also call them 'sunnies' because they love basking in sunny, shallow spots.
description: The pumpkinseed is a colorful, plate-shaped freshwater fish that's one of New England's most beautiful sunfish species. These small fish typically grow 4-8 inches long and have a compressed, almost circular body that looks like it was flattened from the sides. Their scales shimmer with brilliant blues, greens, and golds, while their most famous feature is a bright orange-red ear flap that makes them easy to spot. You'll often see them cruising in shallow, weedy areas of ponds and lakes.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright orange-red ear flap (called an opercular flap) stands out like a tiny flame behind the gill cover, often with a thin black border

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deep, compressed body that feels surprisingly solid and muscular when handled, almost pancake-flat from the sides

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Shimmering blue-green back with golden-yellow sides covered in wavy lines and spots that look like watercolor paint

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Orange pectoral fins and yellow-orange belly fins, with a spiny dorsal fin that feels sharp to the touch

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, terminal mouth that opens at the front of the head, perfect for picking small insects and crustaceans

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Palm-sized fish, typically 4-8 inches long and fitting comfortably in your hand

habitat: Pumpkinseeds thrive in shallow, weedy areas of ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. They prefer warm water with plenty of aquatic vegetation, fallen logs, and rocky areas where they can find cover and hunt for small prey. You'll often spot them in water less than 10 feet deep, especially around docks, lily pads, and marshy shorelines.

seasonality.spring: Males develop brighter colors and create circular nests in sandy or gravelly shallow areas, aggressively defending their territory with flared gills and spread fins.
seasonality.summer: Most active and easiest to spot as they feed heavily in warm, shallow water. Colors are at their most vibrant, especially the orange ear flaps.
seasonality.fall: Still actively feeding but beginning to move to slightly deeper water. Colors remain bright but feeding activity starts to slow as water temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Move to deeper water and become less active, though they can still be caught through ice fishing in deeper parts of their lakes and ponds.

funFact: Male pumpkinseeds are devoted dads who fan their eggs with their tails for up to a week, creating a constant water current that prevents fungus from growing on the developing babies—they beat their tails over 1,000 times per hour without taking a break!
confusionNotes: Pumpkinseeds are most often confused with bluegills, but remember 'orange ears on pumpkinseeds'—bluegills have dark blue-black ear flaps while pumpkinseeds have that distinctive bright orange-red ear flap. Redbreast sunfish also have reddish coloring, but their entire belly and throat are bright red, not just the ear flap.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sunfish,' pumpkinseeds are not related to the massive ocean sunfish (mola mola)—they're freshwater fish in the sunfish family, named for their habit of sunning themselves in shallow, warm water. The many common names like 'punkie,' 'sunny,' and 'kivver' reflect how widespread and beloved these colorful fish are across different New England communities.
compareHints: Among New England's sunfish, pumpkinseeds are the only ones with that signature bright orange-red ear flap. Bluegills have dark ear flaps and more muted colors, while redbreast sunfish have red bellies but longer, more pointed ear flaps. Green sunfish are more olive-colored with a larger mouth, and warmouth have a more bass-like appearance with teeth on their tongue.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's sunfish family, bluegills are distinguished by their prominent blue gill covers and larger mouths compared to pumpkinseeds, lack the long ear flaps of redbreast sunfish, and have a more rounded body shape than the elongated green sunfish.
Compared to its sunfish cousins, the redbreast has the most prominent reddish-orange coloration on its underside and the longest, darkest ear flap without bright borders.
Green sunfish have a much larger mouth than their sunfish cousins - bigger than bluegills, pumpkinseeds, or redbreast sunfish.
Unlike bluegill and pumpkinseed with their bright colors and small mouths, warmouth are drab and big-mouthed.
